title: Retiring from music and Marshall Stearns' Music Inn
summary: He recalls Music Inn sessions and wonders about the tapes; he withholds his discography.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Well, prior to that, you know, I retired right after I think '57 or '58 and, you know...I was in and out of music so much...I went up to Music Inn when Marshall Stearns had this Music Inn...they had these things, and I believe that some of the works of some of the schools in New Jersey--I think it's Rutgers--that have this New York Jazz Institute, I believe it was called. And I was a good friend of Marshall's...and I was just wondering, what ever happened to all of those tapes and things. I'm sure they had to be taping it.
Well, I'll take a look and see. If they were taped, we should have them.

Yeah. But anyway, we had...we really had some...we had Milt Jackson and they had a cross section of people, you know. James P. Johnson, Mahalia Jackson and any person you name, they had up there. And sometimes, you know, you have to make records of activities, much against the will of the person, but in the end it may prove to be the history. I know that for any number of years I wouldn't allow writers to put my discography in their books, 'cause they wasn't giving me any of it...I'm commercial, you see, and I want some money for... 'cause I know that there's money in this because I know both sides of the fence. I know as an impresario and I know as an artist. I know there's money, and you can give a person something.
